newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea Kim's aides deny taking bribes from Hanbo.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea Kim's aides deny taking bribes from Hanbo.

text.p: A former minister and three close aides to South Korean President Kim Young-sam on Monday admitted receiving money from the founder of the insolvent Hanbo Group, but denied taking bribes.
On the second day of their trial, former minister Kim Woo-suk said he thought the 200 million won ($223,000) delivered in apple crates was just a gift from Chung Tae-soo to use as political funds.

"I received the money from Chung Tae-soo but I thought it was simply a donation to political funds," Kim told the court. "But it was wrong of me to take the money considering I was a construction minister at the time."
He is charged with receiving bribes in return for setting up roads leading to Hanbo's steel mills.
Hanbo Steel Co, South Korea's second-biggest steel maker and flagship of the Hanbo Group, collapsed in January after racking up $5.8 billion in largely unsecured loans.

Three ruling party legislators and close aides to President Kim, Hong In-gil, Hwang Byung-tai and Chung Jae-chull also admitted receiving from gifts in cash from the Hanbo founder. But they denied allegations they were bribed.
Chung Tae-soo, his chief accountant, an opposition legislator and three top bankers are also on trial.

Among the bankers in custody, Sheen Kwang-shik, the former president of Korea First Bank, Hanbo's main creditor, said he received his first apple crate of 200 million won when he became head of the bank. Having received it the first time, Sheen said it was difficult to turn it down the second time.
Sheen said he tried in vain to return the cash but eventually used it for his daughter's wedding.
The eight defendants accused of receiving bribes gave similar testimony, describing the money they received as gifts.
Chung Tae-soo's questioning was postponed to April 14 when the court reconvenes.
His testimony is eagerly awaited in the hope that he will divulge the top influence peddlers who helped him win massive loans.

The prosecution reopened the Hanbo investigation almost 10 days ago after opposition politicians dismissed it as a whitewash, in which major players emerged unscathed. Over the weekend, the prosecution said it had uncovered evidence that Chung embezzled an additional 30 billion won in cash.
His son, Chung Bo-keun, was also arrested on Friday accused of pocketing about 37 billion won.

The prosecution said they would seize the Chung family's assets to pay off previously evaded taxes of 432.7 billion won and "end the bad practice of the past when businessmen survived even when their businesses collapsed".
